name: LSM Trees vs B-Trees
intent: The two storage-engine families underneath almost every database: update fixed-size pages in place (B-tree), or append sorted immutable files and merge them later (LSM tree).
scenario: A user-events table takes a heavy write load: thousands of small 128-byte events per second, spread across random users. Then the product needs point reads (the latest events of one user) and range scans (a user's events for a day). We follow one event into a B-tree and into an LSM tree, then read it back.
problem: A disk, an SSD especially, is fast at large sequential writes and slow at many small random ones, and every write must also survive a crash. A structure that keeps keys sorted for fast reads has to put each new row in the right place, which means touching a page somewhere in the middle of the file. The two engine families make opposite choices: pay for it at write time, or pay for it at read time and in background work. Neither is free, and the cost is measured as three amplifications: write (bytes hitting the disk per byte the application wrote), read (pages or files touched per lookup) and space (bytes stored per byte of live data).

howItWorks.title: B-tree: sorted fixed-size pages, updated in place
howItWorks.text: Data lives in pages of a fixed size (4 KB to 16 KB: 4 KB in SQLite and many file systems, 8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB). Inner pages hold separator keys and child pointers, leaves hold rows. A lookup walks root to leaf: with a fan-out (children per page) of a few hundred, three or four page reads cover billions of rows, and the top levels stay in the buffer pool (pages cached in memory), so a point read is usually one disk read. An update finds the leaf, changes it in memory and marks the page dirty.

howItWorks.title: B-tree writes: a log record now, a whole page later
howItWorks.text: Before touching the page the engine appends a record to the write-ahead log, which is what makes the change durable. The dirty page is written back later, at a checkpoint or when it is evicted, and always as a whole page: a 128-byte change costs a 4 KB write, up to 32x amplification for an isolated write, less when several changes hit the same page before it is flushed. A full leaf splits in two, writing the new leaf and rewriting the parent; random keys also scatter writes across the file.

howItWorks.title: LSM tree: log, memtable, immutable sorted files
howItWorks.text: A write is appended to the write-ahead log (sequential) and inserted into the memtable, a sorted in-memory structure such as a skip list. When the memtable reaches its size limit (tens of MB) it is written out in one sequential pass as an SSTable: an immutable sorted file with a block index and a bloom filter. Nothing is ever modified in place. An update is just a newer version of the key and a delete is a tombstone marker; the older versions are still on disk.

howItWorks.title: LSM reads: newest to oldest, with filters to skip files
howItWorks.text: A lookup checks the memtable, then the files from newest to oldest and stops at the first version of the key. Each file's key range, its bloom filter (a small in-memory structure that answers 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here'; about 10 bits per key gives roughly a 1% false-positive rate) and its index live in memory, so most files that do not hold the key are skipped without any disk read. A range scan cannot use bloom filters: it has to open every file whose range overlaps and merge the streams.

howItWorks.title: Compaction: merge files to bound reads, at a write cost
howItWorks.text: Without cleanup the number of files, and the read cost, would grow forever. Compaction merges sorted files into larger ones, keeps only the newest version of each key and finally drops tombstones once nothing older can hide below them. Size-tiered compaction merges files of similar size: low write amplification, but several overlapping files and temporary doubling of space. Leveled compaction keeps one non-overlapping sorted run per level, each about 10x the previous (RocksDB's default): fewer files per read and little wasted space, but each byte is rewritten once per level, so write amplification is several times higher.

howItWorks.title: Choose by the amplification you can afford
howItWorks.text: B-tree: low and predictable read cost, scans over adjacent leaves, but a page rewrite per random write and about 30 to 40% free space inside pages. LSM tree: very high ingest rates, compression-friendly dense files and cheap negative lookups, paid for with background compaction I/O, read latency that varies with the file layout, and space that fluctuates. The tuning knobs (size ratio, filters, compaction style) move the cost between the three amplifications; they never remove it.

pros: B-tree: a point lookup is a short, bounded walk (typically one disk read once inner pages are cached) and scans follow adjacent leaves
B-tree: mature, predictable latency, and in-place updates keep the data in one place with no background merge debt
LSM: writes are sequential appends, so ingest throughput is high and flash wear is lower, with write amplification often a fraction of a B-tree's for small random writes
LSM: files are dense and immutable, so they compress well and are easy to snapshot, back up and ship to replicas
LSM: bloom filters make lookups of missing keys nearly free
cons: B-tree: every small random write rewrites a whole page, pages sit partly empty after splits (typically 65 to 70% full), and random writes fragment the file
B-tree: heavy concurrent writes contend on hot pages and need latching, and a crash during a page write needs a log or doublewrite buffer to repair a torn page
LSM: compaction burns disk bandwidth and CPU in the background, and when it falls behind reads slow down and writes stall
LSM: reads touch several places, range scans cannot use bloom filters, and space amplification varies, with size-tiered compaction briefly needing up to about twice the live data
LSM: deleted data lingers until a compaction reaches it, which matters for retention and privacy deletes
whenToUse: LSM tree: write-heavy ingestion of events, metrics, messages or time series (Cassandra, HBase, RocksDB, LevelDB, ScyllaDB, ClickHouse parts)
LSM tree: data that compresses well, or flash storage where fewer, larger writes extend device life
B-tree: read-heavy or mixed OLTP (many small transactions) with point lookups and range scans, where predictable latency matters (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, SQLite)
B-tree: workloads of in-place updates to hot rows, where the buffer pool absorbs repeated changes to the same pages
whenNotToUse: LSM tree: a small data set with a modest write rate, where a B-tree's write cost is invisible and its reads are simpler
LSM tree: strict tail-latency targets on a store that cannot spare headroom for compaction
B-tree: sustained random-write ingest well beyond what the device can absorb as page rewrites
Either: choosing by reputation instead of measuring the real read/write mix, key distribution and value size
pitfalls: Judging by a benchmark that never reaches steady state: an LSM tree looks wonderful until compaction debt accumulates, and a B-tree looks wonderful until the data no longer fits in the buffer pool
Under-provisioned compaction: when the write rate exceeds what compaction can merge, files pile up, reads degrade and the engine finally stalls writes

Deleting or expiring massive amounts of data in an LSM store: tombstones are extra writes, are read past by scans, and the space only returns after compaction; time-window data is better dropped as whole files or partitions
Reading the stats wrong: write amplification of 20x is not bad for a B-tree that batches page writes at checkpoints, and a 10x LSM figure may be the price of low space and read amplification
Turning off or undersizing bloom filters on a read-heavy LSM table, so every missing-key lookup opens every overlapping file
Forgetting that a B-tree needs its log too: in-place page writes are not atomic, and a torn page without a write-ahead log or doublewrite buffer is corruption
Disabling the LSM write-ahead log for speed: the memtable is only in memory, so a crash loses every write since the last flush

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Issues the writes, point reads and range scans.

roles.label: B-tree page
roles.description: A fixed-size leaf page updated in place and rewritten whole.

roles.label: Write-ahead log
roles.description: Sequential append-only record of each change, for durability.

roles.label: Memtable
roles.description: Sorted in-memory buffer of the newest writes in an LSM tree.

roles.label: SSTables
roles.description: Immutable sorted files on disk, each with an index and a bloom filter.

roles.label: Compaction
roles.description: Background job that merges files, keeps the newest versions and drops tombstones.

quiz.question: A table takes 20,000 inserts per second of 128-byte events with random keys, on an SSD. A B-tree engine writes one 8 KB page per insert in the worst case and the disk is saturated. Why would an LSM engine cope better with the same load?
options: It keeps the data in memory, so nothing needs to reach the disk quickly
It updates rows in place using smaller pages, so each insert writes fewer bytes
It buffers writes in memory and flushes large sorted files sequentially
It compacts continuously, so fewer pages are needed overall
quiz.explanation: An LSM engine turns many small random writes into one sequential write of a whole memtable, so the write amplification for small events is lower. It still writes everything to disk, and compaction is extra work, not the reason writes are cheap. Smaller in-place pages would still be random writes.

quiz.question: A read-heavy LSM table is used to check whether an id has been seen before, and most checks find nothing. Latency is high and profiling shows each check opens many overlapping files. Bloom filters were turned off to save memory. Without changing the write path, what is the best fix?
options: Increase the memtable size so fewer files are created
Disable the write-ahead log to speed up flushes
Add a read replica for these checks
Turn the bloom filters back on for the table
quiz.explanation: A bloom filter lets a lookup skip files that cannot contain the key, which is exactly what missing-key checks need. A larger memtable only reduces file count somewhat, and removing the log risks losing writes without helping reads. A read replica only moves the same slow checks elsewhere.

quiz.question: A team removes six months of old rows from an LSM store by issuing a delete for every key. Disk usage goes up, and scans of recent data become slower. What explains this, and what should they do next time?
options: Tombstones linger until compaction, so keep data in time windows and drop whole files
Deletes rewrite pages in place and fragment the file, so rebuild the index after each purge
The write-ahead log still holds the deleted rows, so truncate it after deleting them
Bloom filters keep deleted keys alive, so rebuild every filter after each large purge
quiz.explanation: In an LSM tree a delete is a new write, and scans have to read past the tombstones until compaction finally removes them. Deletes do not rewrite pages in place, and neither the log nor the filters keep the deleted rows alive. Data with a natural expiry is better organised by time window so a whole file or partition can be dropped.
